awd_titl_txt: Conference: Travel support for trainees to attend Dynein 2025; Ann Arbor, Michigan; 22-24 July 2025
awd_abstract_narration:
The Dynein 2025 meeting is an international conference dedicated exclusively to the study of dynein motor proteins. Dyneins are large proteins that act as cellular engines, driving directed movement along protein tracks called microtubules. They are essential for a wide range of processes within cells, such as transporting internal components and enabling the movement of structures like cilia and flagella. Held in Ann Arbor, Michigan, from July 22–24, 2025, this meeting provides a crucial forum for experts to discuss the latest discoveries and future directions in this rapidly advancing field. It offers a unique opportunity for researchers to share unpublished findings, initiate collaborations, and debate new models. A key focus is fostering the next generation of US-based scientists; students, post-doctoral fellows, and young faculty will present their work, gain visibility, and connect with established leaders in the field through presentations, poster sessions, and networking opportunities. This in-person gathering is the first since 2016, emphasizing vibrant, interactive discussions to drive the field forward.

The Dynein 2025 conference focuses on recent, often unpublished, transformative advances in dynein biology, building on breakthroughs in cryo-EM, biophysics, and cell biology. The program will highlight new insights into dynein architecture, regulation, and diverse cellular roles. Key discussion areas include near-atomic resolution structures of different classes of dyneins, mechanistic understanding of axonemal dynein assembly and ciliary beating, and innovative reconstitution studies revealing how dyneins coordinate with regulatory molecules. The meeting unites researchers employing multidisciplinary approaches, including single-molecule biophysics, structural biology, advanced cell imaging, genetics, and computational modeling, to address unresolved questions in the field. Topics range from the mechanisms controlling cytoplasmic dynein activity and cargo interactions to the physical principles underlying motor function, intraflagellar transport, and axonemal dynein regulation. Discussions are designed to bridge gaps between structural models, single-molecule mechanics, and physiological contexts, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration and novel hypotheses. This uniquely focused meeting facilitates candid exchanges on emerging work and ideas, providing a critical platform for synthesizing progress across the dynein field.

This award is funded by the Cellular Dynamics and Function Cluster of the Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences in the Directorate for Biological Sciences.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
NSF support helped 32 trainees participate in Dynein 2025, an international scientific meeting held July 22-24, 2025, in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The meeting focused exclusively on dynein motors, which are molecular motors that move along protein tracks called microtubules inside cells. Some dynein motors transport cellular materials, while others drive the beating of cilia and flagella, which are structures that help cells move or move fluid across cell surfaces. We organized the meeting to connect researchers studying how these motors are built, how they are controlled, and how they function in cells.

The meeting brought together 71 participants. The meeting had six scientific sessions and 30 posters were presented. It was the first in-person gathering in this meeting series since 2016. Researchers discussed how dynein motors attach to cellular materials and generate force, how they support transport within nerve cells and cilia, and how they coordinate ciliary movement. The program also addressed the role that dynein dysfunction plays in human disease. The meeting provided a forum to compare research approaches and to discuss models of how dynein motors work.

A central goal was to provide a setting for scientists to share and discuss new, unpublished work. Talks and poster sessions allowed participants to exchange ideas, outline emerging results, and discuss unresolved questions directly with other researchers. All attendants ate breakfast and lunch together to provide additional opportunities for informal scientific conversations and provided opportunities to establish future collaborations.

We used the NSF award to offset attendance costs for 32 students and postdoctoral fellows. Eight trainees spoke in the program. These presentations gave trainees experience communicating their work to an international audience, while the broader meeting provided opportunities to learn from established investigators and other trainees.

A key goal of the award was to support the next generation of scientists. The award made participation in this specialized international meeting more accessible to trainees, including students and postdoctoral fellows at US institutions. By reducing attendance costs, we supported trainees in presenting their work alongside established investigators and gaining visibility within the field. Poster sessions and informal discussions provided opportunities to develop professional relationships and learn from researchers with different scientific approaches. These experiences supported the scientific training and professional development of students and postdoctoral fellows.
